text: Chemical disorder opens an enormous space for materials design. When many elements share a crystal lattice, both their composition and their atomic arrangement can be varied. The number of possibilities quickly becomes too large to explore one material at a time.

We develop computational and AI methods that learn from these large chemical spaces and propose new materials for energy production, chemical manufacturing, nuclear technology, and extreme environments. A major goal is to move beyond brute-force screening toward models that can propose materials with the chemistry and atomic structure needed for a particular function.

Students can follow a material from computational prediction through synthesis and experimental testing. Our current research centers on new methods for learning and generating chemical disorder, hydrogen production, and nuclear energy.

directions.title: Learning and generating chemical disorder
text: AI is changing what is possible in materials design. Chemical spaces that are far too large to explore one material at a time can instead be learned by models that identify patterns and generate new candidates. Disordered materials make this problem especially challenging because a single composition can contain many different atomic arrangements. We want AI models that learn both which elements belong in a material and how those elements arrange themselves at the atomic scale.

Students in this area work at the intersection of materials science, physics, AI, and scientific computing. Projects can involve electronic-structure calculations, machine-learned potentials, molecular dynamics, large-scale materials data, generative modeling, and the development of open scientific software.

directions.title: Hydrogen production
text: Hydrogen is a backbone of the energy and chemical industries. It is used at enormous scale in refining, chemical manufacturing, and fertilizer production, and its role is expanding across energy technologies. Most hydrogen production relies on natural gas, tying its economics to natural-gas prices. New production routes can diversify how and where hydrogen is made.

We design materials for producing hydrogen from water using electricity or heat. Our work combines AI and computational materials design with experimental synthesis and testing. Machine learning helps us explore complex alloys as alternatives to precious-metal catalysts, and we use first-principles calculations to understand how atomic arrangement changes catalytic behavior. We also design multicomponent redox oxides for thermochemical water splitting.
Students working in this area encounter catalysis, electronic structure, thermodynamics, machine learning, materials synthesis, and experimental characterization.

directions.title: Nuclear energy: fission and fusion
text: Growing electricity demand will require enormous amounts of reliable power. Nuclear fission is one of the few technologies already capable of supplying electricity continuously at that scale. Its continued and expanded use requires materials that can operate safely for long periods and durable approaches to nuclear waste.

We study materials for both sides of this challenge. Our work includes high-temperature materials for demanding reactor environments and new waste forms that immobilize radioactive elements for very long times. In recent work, we demonstrated that iodine can be incorporated directly into the crystal lattice of a pyrochlore waste form.

Fusion presents one of the most ambitious challenges in energy science: reproducing on Earth the reactions that power the stars and turning them into a practical source of energy. Doing that is also a materials problem. Components near the plasma must survive conditions encountered almost nowhere else in engineering. We investigate chemically complex materials for these environments, including materials used near plasmas and in the production of fusion fuel.
Research in nuclear materials spans phase stability, defect chemistry, extreme-environment materials, first-principles calculations, machine learning, synthesis, and characterization.
